title: Everest Heli Tour or Base Camp Trek: Which Suits You
summary: Choose the Everest heli tour if you have one morning, older family members or no time to train: it costs from US$1,190 a seat and lasts 4–5 hours. Choose the 12–14 day base camp trek if you want to walk to 5,364 m through Sherpa villages, from US$1,390. A trek with a helicopter return splits the difference.
meta_description: Everest heli tour vs Everest Base Camp trek: days, cost, altitude, fitness and weather compared, plus the middle option of a trek with a heli return.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Both trips show you Everest, Lhotse, Nuptse and Ama Dablam at close range. The difference is how you get there and what you see on the way. The helicopter flies from Kathmandu up the Khumbu valley, circles base camp and lands for breakfast at Hotel Everest View, all in one morning. The trek walks 65 km each way from Lukla through Namche Bazaar, Tengboche and Dingboche, sleeping in teahouse lodges and climbing slowly to base camp at 5,364 m and Kala Patthar at 5,644 m.

Time and health usually decide it. If you have a week or less, are travelling with parents over 60 or children under 10, or have a heart or lung condition, the trek is not a realistic option, and the helicopter is. If you have two weeks, walk regularly at home and want to earn the view, trek.

There is no wrong answer here. Plenty of people take the helicopter on a first visit to Nepal and return years later to walk, and trekkers who have already been to base camp often fly back with their parents to show them the mountain.

sections.heading: Side by side: days, cost and altitude
paras: The figures come from our own packages and are per person on twin sharing. The heli price is for a shared seat; a private charter for up to five costs roughly US$5,000–6,500 per helicopter.

The headline prices hide some differences. The trek price covers flights, lodges, meals, guide, porter and permits, but you also need a down jacket, boots and a sleeping bag if you do not own them, tips of roughly US$150–250 per trekker, and drinks and charging fees that rise with altitude. The heli price covers almost everything except your Kathmandu hotel. Both need travel insurance; for the trek, make sure the policy covers helicopter evacuation up to 6,000 m.

sections.heading: What the heli tour gives you, and does not
paras: The morning starts with a hotel pickup at about 5:45 am and a 6:30 am take-off. The helicopter refuels at Lukla, follows the Dudh Koshi past Namche and Tengboche, circles above base camp and the Khumbu Icefall, and when rules and weather allow, lands on the Kala Patthar ridge at about 5,550 m for 10–15 minutes. The return stops at Hotel Everest View at 3,880 m for breakfast facing Everest and Ama Dablam, and you are back in Kathmandu between 10:30 am and noon.

Two things to know before you book. First, landings change: tourist helicopters are generally not allowed to land at base camp itself, and permission for Kala Patthar has come and gone, so check current status before you travel. Second, thin air limits payload, so above 5,000 m the helicopter often carries only two or three passengers and shuttles the group. What the tour cannot give you is the Khumbu on foot: the monasteries, lodges and slow change from pine forest to glacier.

sections.heading: What the trek asks of you
paras: The classic trek flies to Lukla at 2,860 m, then walks for 8 days to Gorak Shep with acclimatisation days at Namche Bazaar (3,440 m) and Dingboche (4,410 m). Most days are 5–6 hours on foot; the base camp day and the Kala Patthar sunrise are 7–8 hours each. It is graded Challenging for altitude and distance, not for technical climbing. Our 14-day version adds a third acclimatisation day at Chhukung, which improves the odds of reaching the top feeling well.

Lodges are simple above Namche, with shared toilets and unheated rooms, and nights at Gorak Shep fall to −10 °C or lower in late autumn. Headache and poor sleep are common above 4,000 m. A licensed guide is part of every package, and you need the Sagarmatha National Park fee and the local Khumbu permit, both included. In peak months, Lukla flights have operated from Ramechhap, 4–5 hours by road from Kathmandu; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Two middle options
paras: Many travellers do not fit neatly into either group. These two trips combine walking and flying.
list: EBC trek with heli return, 11 days from US$2,190: walk up with full acclimatisation, climb Kala Patthar at sunrise, then fly from Gorak Shep to Kathmandu the same morning, saving three days of descent and sore knees

Everest View trek, 7 days from US$990: walk from Lukla to Namche, Hotel Everest View and Khumjung, with 3–6 hour days and no nights above 3,800 m; it suits families and older walkers who want some trail time

sections.heading: Who should choose which
paras: These are the matches we make most often when travellers ask us to choose for them.
list: Indian families with grandparents or young children: the 3-day package with the heli tour, Pashupatinath aarti and Boudhanath, with the landing kept at 3,880 m
Couples with one free day in Kathmandu: the shared-seat heli tour, with a spare morning in case of cloud
Fit adults aged 18–60 with two weeks: the 14-day trek, or 12 days if you have trekked at altitude before
Trekkers with weak knees or a fixed flight home: the trek with heli return
Photographers: the heli for the aerial view of the Khumbu Glacier, the trek for sunrise on Kala Patthar
People with heart or lung disease, pregnant women and infants: neither the high landing nor the trek; ask about the Everest mountain flight instead

sections.heading: Weather affects both choices
paras: Helicopters and Lukla planes both fly by sight. On a typical good day the sky is clear at dawn, cloud forms in the lower valleys by 9 or 10 am, and the peaks disappear by noon. For the heli tour, keep at least one spare morning in Kathmandu; for the trek, keep one spare day before your international flight. October to December and March to April are the steadiest months for flying, while June to August makes both uncertain. Pricing, landing rules and permit fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is the Everest heli tour worth it compared with the trek?
faqs.a: It is worth it if you cannot spend two weeks or cannot trek to 5,000 m for health reasons. In 4–5 hours you see Everest base camp from the air and eat breakfast facing Everest at 3,880 m. You miss the Sherpa villages and the sense of walking there, which is why fit travellers with time usually prefer the trek.

faqs.q: Which is cheaper, the Everest heli tour or the EBC trek?
faqs.a: A shared heli seat starts at about US$1,190 (₹1,05,000), and our 12-day trek starts at about US$1,390 (₹1,22,000). The trek also needs gear, tips and spare days, so its real cost is higher. A private helicopter costs US$5,000–6,500 for up to five people, which can match the per-seat price for a family of five.

faqs.q: Can senior citizens do the Everest helicopter tour?
faqs.a: Most healthy seniors can, and many grandparents take it because the trek is not possible for them. People with heart disease, uncontrolled blood pressure or lung conditions should speak to a doctor and stay at the 3,880 m breakfast stop rather than land above 5,000 m. Our 3-day family package keeps the landing at Hotel Everest View for this reason.

faqs.q: Does the Everest helicopter land at base camp?
faqs.a: As we understand it, tourist helicopters are generally not allowed to land at Everest Base Camp except for rescue. When permitted and safe, they land on the Kala Patthar ridge at about 5,550 m for 10–15 minutes, otherwise they circle base camp and land at Hotel Everest View. Landing rules have changed several times, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How fit do I need to be for the Everest Base Camp trek?
faqs.a: You should be able to walk 5–6 hours with a light pack on hilly ground for several days running. Train for 8–12 weeks with long walks, stair climbing and some cardio. Fitness does not protect you from altitude sickness, so the itinerary's acclimatisation days matter as much as your training. Anyone with heart or lung conditions should see a doctor first.
